What to Do After a Slip and Fall Accident in Denver

The moments right after a fall often carry as much weight as the legal work that follows. Quick action may help protect both health and legal rights, and the following steps may be worth taking as soon as possible:
Seek medical attention right away, even if injuries seem minor at first
Report the fall to the property owner, manager, or building staff
Photograph the hazard, the surrounding area, and any visible injuries
Collect names and contact information from anyone who witnessed the fall
Avoid giving a recorded statement to the property owner’s insurer
Contact a
Denver slip and fall lawyer
before accepting any settlement offer

Each of these steps may preserve evidence that tends to disappear quickly, whether a wet floor gets mopped, a broken step gets repaired, or a witness moves away. Understanding what caused the fall in the first place is the next piece of that evidence.
Common Causes of Slip and Fall Accidents in Denver
Slip and fall accidents happen every day in Denver’s parking lots, retail stores, apartment complexes, and government buildings. The most common causes include the following:
Snow, ice, and wet spots on sidewalks and in parking lots
Loose flooring or carpeting
Uneven sidewalks and walking surfaces
Wet or freshly polished floors without warning signage
Debris and clutter left in walkways
Exposed electrical cords
Poor lighting in stairwells and hallways
Poorly maintained escalators and elevators
Potholes and weather-related pavement damage
Denver’s freeze-thaw winter cycles make snow and ice removal a particularly common factor in local claims, and the injuries that follow those falls can be just as varied as their causes.
Common Slip and Fall Injuries and Their Long-Term Effects
The consequences of a fall can range from minor bruising to permanent, life-altering harm. Common injuries may include the following:
Head and brain injuries, including traumatic brain injury
Spinal cord injuries, fractured vertebrae, and paralysis
Broken bones and fractures
Bruising and lacerations
Scarring
Wrongful death

Many of these injuries carry long-term consequences well beyond the initial hospital visit. A hip fracture, for example, can lead to reduced mobility, extended rehabilitation, and, in some cases, fatal complications for older victims; this risk is made more pressing by the frequency of falls. According to the
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

, over 14 million, or 1 in 4, older adults report falling every year. Younger victims are not immune either, since spinal cord injuries and traumatic brain injuries can permanently affect a person’s ability to work and live independently.

A preventable hazard on someone else’s property that caused an injury may open the door to compensation covering both current and future costs, making it essential to identify every responsible party.
Who Can Be Held Liable for a Slip and Fall Accident in Colorado?

Collecting compensation for a slip and fall injury requires correctly identifying every liable party, and the property owner is not always the only one responsible. Common defendants in Denver slip and fall cases include the following:
Private Property Owners:
A homeowner’s insurance policy often covers injuries caused by a property defect on private land.
Lessees:
The person listed on a rental lease may be responsible for injuries occurring inside a rented home.
Landlords:
A landlord typically maintains common areas such as stairwells and parking lots and may be liable for hazards there.
Companies and Corporations:
Businesses can be held vicariously liable when an employee’s negligence, such as failing to clean up a spill, causes an injury.
Government Entities:
Claims involving the City of Denver or the State of Colorado are subject to unique procedural rules and shorter notice deadlines.

Identifying every liable party from the outset helps ensure a claim reflects the full picture of responsibility, a process that runs directly through Colorado’s premises liability laws. For anyone unsure who else might share in that responsibility,
contact us
for a free consultation to discuss it further.
Colorado Premises Liability Laws and Slip and Fall Claims

Slip and fall claims fall under a broader area of law called premises liability. In Colorado, these laws determine how much responsibility a property owner has for keeping visitors safe, and that responsibility often depends on why the visitor was on the property in the first place. This is a good starting point for understanding whether a claim exists.
Property Owner Duties Under Colorado Law
Colorado law requires property owners to take reasonable steps to keep their property safe for lawful visitors. In practice, this means property owners must:
Fix hazards they know about, or should have discovered through routine inspection
Warn visitors when a hazard cannot be fixed right away
Check the property regularly for risks a careful owner would notice

A business that does not salt an icy entrance, a landlord who ignores a broken stairwell railing, or a store that leaves a spill unaddressed for hours may all fail to meet this standard. How strict the standard is can also depend on the visitor’s legal status on the property, an issue Colorado courts examine closely in premises liability cases.
Invitees, Licensees, and Trespassers in Colorado Premises Liability Cases
Colorado law places every visitor into one of three categories, and each one receives a different level of protection:
Invitees:

Customers and other visitors invited onto a property for business purposes receive the highest level of protection. Property owners must take reasonable steps to identify and fix hazards on their own.
Licensees:
Property owners must warn social guests and similar visitors about known, nonobvious dangers.
Trespassers:

People on the property without permission receive the least protection. Property owners generally need only avoid intentionally causing harm, though this protection narrows further when children may wander onto the property.
Determining which category applies to an injured visitor is often the first legal question our
Denver slip and fall lawyers
address, as it sets the direction the rest of the claim will take.
How to Prove Negligence in a Denver Slip and Fall Case
Proving fault is often the most difficult part of any slip and fall claim. Establishing negligence generally requires showing one of the following:
The property owner caused the dangerous condition and did nothing to repair it, block it off, or warn visitors
The property owner knew about the hazard and failed to correct it, block it off, or alert visitors
The property owner should have known about the hazard, since a reasonable person in the same position would have discovered it, and failed to act

Negligence means the property owner did not act as a reasonable and prudent party would have under similar circumstances. Gathering photographs, incident reports, and witness statements early in the process helps build the evidentiary foundation these claims require, though insurers will often seek to shift some of that responsibility back onto the injured person. At
Dormer Harpring
, our
Denver slip and fall lawyers
handle that evidence gathering directly, working to build the strongest possible foundation for a claim from the earliest stages.
Comparative Negligence in Colorado Slip and Fall Claims
Even when a property owner bears most of the responsibility for a fall, an insurer will often argue the injured person contributed to the accident. Under
Colorado Revised Statutes § 13-21-111
, an injured person can still recover compensation as long as their share of fault remains below 50 percent, though the court reduces the award by that percentage.

A person found 20 percent at fault, for example, would recover 80 percent of the total damages awarded. Insurance companies frequently raise distraction, inattention, or improper footwear to increase this percentage, which is why thorough documentation and legal representation are important from the earliest stages of a claim.
What Compensation Can You Recover After a Slip and Fall Injury?

Once fault is established, compensation in a slip and fall claim should reflect both current expenses and the losses that continue well after the initial injury. Typical categories of damages include the following:
Current and future medical expenses
Lost income and reduced earning capacity
Pain and suffering
Mental and emotional trauma
Physical therapy and rehabilitation costs
Wrongful death-related costs
Punitive damages, in cases involving especially reckless or willful conduct by the property owner

No two slip and fall cases carry the same value, since the amount depends on the severity of the injury, the strength of the evidence, and how clearly liability can be established. Strong documentation, from medical records to photographs of the hazard to witness statements, plays a direct role in supporting each of these categories once an insurance company begins reviewing a claim.
Insurance Company Tactics in Slip and Fall Claims

Insurance adjusters handling slip and fall claims are trained to protect their company’s bottom line, not the injured person’s recovery. Common tactics include requesting a recorded statement early, before the full extent of an injury is known, and using any inconsistency against the claim later. Adjusters may also argue the hazard was open and obvious, that the injured person was distracted, or that the injury existed before the fall occurred. Early settlement offers often arrive before medical treatment concludes, allowing the insurer to close a claim before its true value becomes clear.
Recognizing these tactics early may help protect a claim from being undervalued or dismissed outright. A
Denver slip and fall lawyer
can push back on these tactics, from declining a recorded statement to holding off on any settlement offer until the full scope of an injury is known.
What Is the Statute of Limitations on a Slip and Fall Case in Colorado?

Colorado has case filing deadlines, or statutes of limitations, that place a time limit on the right to file a lawsuit in civil court. Colorado usually provides two years from the date on which a slip and fall accident occurred for injured people to file a claim. After that time elapses, a slip and fall claim expires.

An exception may arise when a slip and fall accident causes fatal injuries. A deadly injury case, or wrongful death case, expires two years from the date of death, which may differ from the date of the slip and fall accident. A
Denver wrongful death lawyer
can help with statute of limitation issues.
Another possible exception is when the responsible party is a governmental entity. Cases involving government entities have shorter notice deadlines and a series of other strict requirements.
How We Investigate Slip and Fall Cases
A thorough investigation is what allows a claim to withstand these tactics. Depending on the case, the investigation at
Dormer Harpring

Visiting the accident scene when possible to document conditions firsthand
Requesting maintenance logs, incident reports, and surveillance footage before it can be overwritten or discarded
Interviewing witnesses while memories are still fresh
Consulting engineering or safety experts when a hazard involves a structural or code-related issue
Coordinating with treating physicians to document how the fall affected a client’s health
This groundwork helps build a claim based on the actual circumstances of the fall rather than the insurer’s preferred version of events.
Common Types of Denver Slip and Fall Accidents We Handle
Where a fall occurs often determines what evidence matters most and how a claim comes together. At
Dormer Harpring
, we regularly handle the following types of cases:
Grocery Store and Retail Store Falls

Leaking freezer cases, damp entryway mats, and merchandise left in walkways are common causes of falls inside Denver grocery and retail stores. These businesses typically carry commercial liability insurance, and surveillance footage from the store often becomes critical evidence. A pattern of prior complaints or a lack of routine floor inspections can support a negligence claim against the retailer.
Snow and Ice Slip and Fall Accidents

Denver’s freeze-thaw winters create some of the most common slip and fall hazards in the region, from black ice on parking garage ramps to slush that refreezes overnight on building steps. Property owners are expected to clear walkways within a reasonable time after a storm, and a failure to do so can support a premises liability claim. Timing and weather records often play a central role, since an injured person must show the property owner had a reasonable opportunity to address the hazard.
Apartment and Property Maintenance Falls

Loose carpeting, unmarked changes in flooring height, and inadequate lighting in shared hallways frequently cause falls at Denver apartment complexes. Landlords are generally responsible for maintaining common areas, and a documented history of maintenance requests can strengthen a claim. When the injury occurs within a specific unit rather than in a shared space, the tenant’s lease and insurance coverage may also come into play.
Parking Lot and Sidewalk Falls

Uneven pavement, drainage grates, and poorly maintained curb ramps make parking lots and sidewalks frequent sites of Denver slip and fall accidents. Liability can extend to a private business, a property management company, or the City of Denver, depending on where the hazard was located. Claims involving public sidewalks or municipal property have shorter notice deadlines, making timing one of the most important factors in these cases.
How Long Does a Slip and Fall Case Take to Resolve?

Timing affects more than deadlines; it also shapes how long a case takes to resolve. The timeline depends on the severity of the injury, the clarity of liability, and the insurer’s willingness to negotiate in good faith. Straightforward cases with clear fault and minor injuries can be resolved within a few months. However, cases involving serious injuries, disputed liability, or a government defendant often take a year or longer, particularly when the full extent of medical treatment and future care needs must be established before a fair settlement can be reached.

Rushing toward a quick resolution before treatment concludes often means accepting less than a claim is worth, which is precisely why Colorado’s filing deadlines demand attention from the very beginning.
Time Limit to File a Slip and Fall Claim in Colorado
Colorado law imposes a strict time limit on the right to file a slip and fall lawsuit. Under
Colorado Revised Statutes § 13-80-102
, most personal injury claims must be filed within two years from the date of the accident, and missing this deadline typically bars recovery entirely.

Some exceptions may apply, but they are not the rule. If the injured person is a minor, the filing clock generally pauses until they turn 18. If someone is legally incapacitated at the time of the injury, the deadline may pause until competency is restored. Claims against a government entity, such as the City of Denver, come with a much shorter notice deadline, often just six months, along with extra procedural steps. Because these exceptions are narrow, checking with a
Denver slip and fall lawyer
early is the best way to make sure a deadline is not missed.
